arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Samek argued that Congress enacted the statute solely to increase penalties for money laundering conspiracies.
She contended that Congress did not intend to abandon the overt act requirement for these offenses.
Mr. Marcus asserted that the money laundering conspiracy statute does not require proof of an overt act.
He stated that the text of the statute contains no such requirement as a primary reason.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case examines the legal requirements for prosecuting money laundering conspiracies. The core issue is whether the statute mandates proof of an overt act. the sides that brought the case argue this requirement remains in effect. The government contends the statute does not require such proof.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case want the Court to confirm that proving an overt act is mandatory for a money laundering conspiracy conviction.
The government wants the Court to rule that the statute does not require proof of an overt act for such charges.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case argue that Congress intended to preserve the overt act requirement when enacting the specific penalty provisions.
The government argues that the statutory text contains no explicit requirement for proving an overt act in conspiracy cases.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Stevens asked why the statute lists venue options in the alternative if an overt act were always required.
Justice Scalia asked if the cited provision is the only basis for establishing venue in these cases.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the evidentiary burden for federal money laundering conspiracy prosecutions. It clarifies whether prosecutors must demonstrate a specific criminal act. The outcome shapes how courts interpret statutory silence on conspiracy elements. It impacts the scope of federal criminal jurisdiction over financial crimes.
